questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Carnot engine has an efficiency of $50 %$ when its source is at a temperature $327 ° C .$ The temperature of the sink is:
questions.solution:
Efficiency of Carnot engine is given by,

$η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{sink}}{{T}_{source}} ⇒ \dfrac{50}{100} = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{sink}}{\left(327 + 273\right)K} ⇒ {T}_{sink} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 600 = 300K = \left(300 - 273\right) ° C = 27 ° C$

questions.q: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas undergoes a cyclic process as shown in the figure. The total heat supplied to the gas is :
questions.solution:
For a complete cyclic process, the change in internal energy is zero, i.e., $\Delta U = 0$.

According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$.

Therefore, the net heat supplied to the gas is equal to the net work done by the gas: $\Delta Q = \Delta W$.

The net work done $\Delta W$ is given by the area enclosed by the cycle on the $P-V$ diagram.

$\Delta W = \text{Area of rectangle } abcd$

$\Delta W = (P_a - P_d) \times (V_b - V_a)$

$\Delta W = (300 - 100) \times (5 - 2)$

$\Delta W = 200 \times 3 = 600 \text{ J}$

Thus, the total heat supplied to the gas is $600 \text{ J}$.

Answer: $600$ J

questions.q: A container has two chambers of volumes $V_1=2$ litres and $V_2=3$ litres separated by a partition made of a thermal insulator. The chambers contains $n_1=5$ and $n_2=4$ moles of ideal gas at pressures $p_1=1 \mathrm{~atm}$ and $p_2=2 \mathrm{~atm}$, respectively. When the partition is removed, the mixture attains an equilibrium pressure of :
questions.solution:
By energy conservation
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{E}_1+\mathrm{E}_2=\mathrm{E}_{\text{mix }} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{n}_1 \mathrm{f}_1 \mathrm{RT}_1}{2}+\frac{\mathrm{n}_2 \mathrm{f}_2 \mathrm{RT}_2}{2}=\frac{\left(\mathrm{n}_1 \times \mathrm{n}_2\right) \mathrm{fRT}_{\text{mix }}}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{3}{2} \mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{ V}_1+\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{ V}_2=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{P}_{\text{mix }}\left(\mathrm{V}_1+\mathrm{V}_2\right) \\
& \frac{3}{2} \times 1 \times 2+\frac{3}{2} \times 2 \times 3=\frac{3}{2} \times \mathrm{P}_{\text{mix }}(5) \\
& \therefore \mathrm{P}_{\text{mix }}=\frac{8}{5} \\
& \mathrm{P}_{\text{mix }}=1.6 \mathrm{ atm}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric heater supplies heat to a system at a rate of $100$ W. If the system performs work at a rate of $75$ J/s, then the rate at which internal energy increases will be :
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dU}{dt} + \dfrac{dW}{dt}$

Given that the rate of heat supplied is $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 100$ W and the rate of work done by the system is $\dfrac{dW}{dt} = 75$ J/s = $75$ W.

Substituting the values:

$100 = \dfrac{dU}{dt} + 75$

$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 100 - 75 = 25$ W

The rate at which internal energy increases is $25$ W.

Answer: $25$ W

$V ∝ T$

$⇒$ Isobaric process

$W = P ∆ V = nR ∆ T$

questions.q: A gas mixture consists of $2$ moles of ${O}_{2}$ and 4 moles of $Ar$ at temperature $T$. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is ($R$ is universal gas constant)
questions.solution:
For a gas having $n$ moles of molecules with each $f$ degrees of freedom at temperature $TK,$ internal energy is $U = \dfrac{1}{2}nfRT$

$∴$ Total internal energy is

$U = {n}_{1}\dfrac{{f}_{1}}{2}RT + {n}_{2}\dfrac{{f}_{2}}{2}RT$

$= 2 \times \dfrac{5}{2}RT + 4 \times \dfrac{3}{2}RT$

$= 5RT + 6RT$

$U = 11RT$

$\beta =$ coefficient of performance of refrigerator

$η =$ efficiency of heat engine

$\beta = \dfrac{1 - η}{η}$

$= \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{10}}{\dfrac{1}{10}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{9}{10}}{\dfrac{1}{10}}$

$\beta = 9$

$\beta = \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{W}$

$∵ {Q}_{2} =$ heat absorbed from sink and $W =$ work done in a cycle

${Q}_{2} = 9 \times 10 = 90J$

questions.solution:
$\text{P}{\text{V}}^{3} =$ constant polytropic process with $\text{n} = 3$

$\text{C} = {\text{C}}_{\text{v}} + \dfrac{\text{R}}{1 - \text{n}}$

For monoatomic gas : ${\text{C}}_{\text{v}} = \dfrac{3\text{R}}{2}$

$\text{C} = \dfrac{3\text{R}}{2} + \dfrac{\text{R}}{1 - 3}$

$= \dfrac{3\text{R}}{2} - \dfrac{\text{R}}{2}$

$= \dfrac{2\text{R}}{2}$

$\text{C} = \text{R}$

questions.q: A given sample of an ideal gas occupies a volume, $V$ at a pressure, $P$ and absolute temperature,~$T$. The mass of each molecule of the gas is $\text{m}$. Which of the following gives the density of the gas?
questions.solution:
$PV = nRT ⇒ PV = \left(\dfrac{m}{M}\right)RT$

$P = \left(\dfrac{R}{M}\right)\dfrac{m}{V}T ⇒ \dfrac{P}{ρ} = \left(\dfrac{R}{m{N}_{A}}\right)T$

$⇒ \dfrac{P}{ρ} = \dfrac{kT}{m}$

$ρ = \dfrac{Pm}{kT}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
In an adiabatic expansion, the temperature of one mole of an ideal monatomic gas ($\gamma=5/3$) decreases from $60$K to $50$K. The work done by the gas in the process is :
(Take the universal gas constant as $R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The work done by an ideal gas in an adiabatic process is given by the formula:

$W = \dfrac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}$

Given values are:
$n = 1$ mole
$R = 8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$
$T_1 = 60$ K
$T_2 = 50$ K
$\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$W = \dfrac{1 \times 8.3 \times (60 - 50)}{\dfrac{5}{3} - 1}$

$W = \dfrac{8.3 \times 10}{\dfrac{2}{3}}$

$W = \dfrac{83 \times 3}{2}$

$W = \dfrac{249}{2} = 124.5$ J

Answer: $124.5$ J

For engine and refrigeration operating between two same temperature, the relationship between efficiency and coefficient of performance $\beta$,

$η = \dfrac{1}{1 + \beta}$

$\dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \beta} ⇒ \beta = 9$

From the principle of the refrigerator, coefficient of performance is given by the ratio of the amount of energy absorbed from the reservoir to work, i.e.,

$\dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{W} = \beta$

$\dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{10} = 9$

${Q}_{2} = 90J$.

questions.q: Two Carnot engines $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ are operated in series. The engine $A$ receives heat from the source at temperature $T_1$ and rejects the heat to the sink at temperature $T$. The second engine $\mathrm{B}$ receives the heat at temperature $\mathrm{T}$ and rejects to its sink at temperature $T_2$. For what value of $T$ the efficiencies of the two engines are equal:
questions.solution:
We know that efficiency of carnot engine $\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$
Where $T_1=$ temperature of source $T_2=$ temp of $\operatorname{sink}$ For engine $A, n_{\mathrm{A}}=1-\frac{T}{T_1}$ an engine $B, n_{\mathrm{B}}=1-\frac{T_2}{T}$ From question
$\begin{array}{l}
n_A =n_B \\
1-\frac{T}{T_1} =1-\frac{T_2}{T} \\
\Rightarrow \frac{T}{T_1}=\frac{T_2}{T} =\mathrm{T}^2 \\
\Rightarrow \mathrm{T}^2 =\mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{~T}_2 \\
\Rightarrow \mathrm{T} =\sqrt{T_1 T_2}
\end{array}$

In an isothermal process the temperature remains constant

The correct answer is option 1) i.e. In an isochoric process pressure remains constant. - As the change in volume is zero, the work done is zero. \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} Adiabatic process \end{array}$$\begin{array}{l} - It is a process in which no heat is exchanged between the
system and the surrounding i.e. the system is insulated.
- It is represented mathematically as PV= constant \end{array}
EXPLANATION: - An isochoric process is a thermodynamic process that occurs when the change in volume is zero. - Hence the statement 'In an isochoric process pressure remains constant is not true.

questions.question: An engine has an efficiency of $1 / 6$. When the temperature of sink is reduced by $62^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, its efficiency is doubled. Temperatures of the source is:

questions.q: A Carnot engine whose sink is at $300 \mathrm{~K}$ has an efficiency of $40 \%$. By how much should the temperature of source be increased so as to increase its efficiency by $50 \%$ of original efficiency?
questions.solution:
Efficiency of carnot engine =

$\begin{aligned}$& \eta=1-$\frac{T_2}{T_1}$\\
& $\text{$ or $} \quad \frac{T_2}{T_1}=$1-\eta \\
& =1-$\frac{40}{100}=\frac{3}{5}$\\
& \therefore \quad T_1=$\frac{50}{100}$n=$\frac{3}{2}$n \\
& =500 $\mathrm{~K}$\\
& $\begin{array}{l}\text{ New efficiency }$\\
\eta^{\prime}=\eta+$\frac{50}{100} \eta=\frac{3}{2}$ \eta=60 \%
\end{array}$ \\
& \therefore \quad \frac{T_2}{T_1}$=$1-\frac{60}{100}=\frac{2}{5}$\\
& \therefore T_1^{\prime}=$\frac{5}{2}$ \times$T_2=\frac{5}{2}$ \times300=750 $\text{. }\\
&
\end{aligned}

Increase$ in temperature of source\begin{aligned}$& =T_1^{\prime}-T_1 \\
& =750-300=250 \mathrm{~K} .
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: One mole of an ideal monoatomic gas undergoes the process $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow A$ as shown in the graph. The work done during the process is
questions.solution:
Process undergone by 1 mole gas is as shown
For an ideal monoatomic gas, ratio of specific heat $\gamma=\frac{5}{3}$ For adiabatic process $A \rightarrow B$ $p_A V_A^\gamma=p_B V_B^\gamma$ Substituting values of $p_A, p_B$ and $V_B$ from graph, $\Rightarrow \quad 32 \times 10^5 \times V_A^\gamma=1 \times 10^5 \times(1)^\gamma$ $\Rightarrow \quad V_A^\gamma=\left(\frac{1}{32}\right)^\gamma$ Here, $\quad \gamma=\frac{5}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \quad\left(V_A\right)^{\frac{5}{3}}=\frac{1}{32}$ or $V_A=\left(\frac{1}{32}\right)^{\frac{3}{5}}=\frac{1}{\left(2^5\right)^{\frac{3}{5}}}=\frac{1}{8} \mathrm{~m}^3$ Similarly for adiabatic compression $C \rightarrow D$, $p_C V_C^\gamma=p_D V_D^\gamma$ We substitute values from graph, $\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \left(1 \times 10^5\right) \times(8)^{\frac{5}{3}}=\left(32 \times 10^5\right)\left(V_D\right)^{\frac{5}{3}} \\ \Rightarrow & V_D^{5 / 3}=1 \\ \Rightarrow & V_D=1^{3 / 5}=1 \mathrm{~m}^3\end{array}$ Now, Work done in process $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow A$ $=W_{A B}+W_{B C}+W_{C D}+W_{D A}$ Here we substitute work done for adiabatic process, $W_{\text{adiabatic }}=\frac{p_i V_i-p_f V_f}{\gamma-1}$ and work done of isobaric process, $W_{\text{isobaric }}=p\left(V_f-V_i\right)$ so, work done in given cycle $A B C D A$ $=W_{A B}+W_{B C}+W_{C D}+W_{D A}$ $\begin{aligned}= & \frac{\left(p_A V_A-p_B V_B\right)}{\gamma-1}+p_B\left(V_C-V_B\right) \\ & \quad+\left(\frac{p_C V_C-p_D V_D}{\gamma-1}\right)+p_D\left(V_A-V_D\right)\end{aligned}$ Substituting values of pressures and volumes, we get $W_{A B C D A}=\left(\frac{32 \times 10^5 \times \frac{1}{8}-1 \times 10^5 \times 1}{\frac{5}{3}-1}\right)$ $\begin{array}{r}+1 \times 10^5(8-1)+\left(\frac{1 \times 10^5 \times 8-32 \times 10^5 \times 1}{\frac{5}{3}-1}\right) \\ +32 \times 10^5\left(\frac{1}{8}-1\right)\end{array}$ $\begin{aligned}=\frac{3 \times 10^5 \times 3}{2}+7 \times 10^5 & +\frac{-24 \times 10^5 \times 3}{2} \\ & +4 \times 10^5 \times-7=-52.5 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cyclic process is shown in the p-T diagram. Which of the curves show the same process on a $\mathrm{P}$ - $\mathrm{V}$ diagram?
questions.solution:
- Given diagram: P-T graph.
- Using ideal gas law: \(P V=n R T \Rightarrow V=\frac{n R T}{P}\).
So in a \(P-T\) graph we can infer how \(V\) behaves.
Step analysis of cycle \(\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}\) :
- A \(\rightarrow \mathrm{B}\) : Both \(P\) and \(T\) increase proportionally (straight line through origin).
\(\Rightarrow V=\frac{n R T}{P}=\text{ constant. }\)
So \(\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}\) is an isochoric process in \(P-V\).
- \(\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}: T\) constant, \(P\) decreases.
\(\Rightarrow\) Isothermal expansion in \(P-V\).
- \(\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}: P\) constant, \(T\) decreases.
\(\Rightarrow\) Isochoric process in \(P-V\).
So the cycle consists of:
- Isochoric line,
- Isothermal curve,
- Isochoric line.
This matches diagram (2).

questions.q: Helium gas goes through a cycle $ABCDA$ (consisting of two isochoric and two isobaric lines) as shown in figure. The efficiency of this cycle is approximately
questions.solution:
Helium is mono atomic gas, for which
${C}_{V} = \dfrac{3}{2}R . {C}_{p} = \dfrac{5}{2}R$

Work done by the gas in one complete cycle $W =$ area $ABCDA = {p}_{0}{V}_{0}$

From $A to B$, Heat given to gas $= n{C}_{V}\DeltaT$

$= 1 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{2}R\right) \times \DeltaT = \dfrac{3}{2}{V}_{0}\left(\Deltap\right) = \dfrac{3}{2}{V}_{0}{p}_{0}$

From $B to C$, heat given to gas $= n{C}_{p}\DeltaT$

$= 1 \times \left(\dfrac{5}{2}R\right) \times \DeltaT = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(2{p}_{0}\right)\DeltaV = 5{p}_{0}{V}_{0}$

Efficiency of cycle $= \dfrac{Workdonebythegas / cycle}{Totalheatgiventogas / cycle}$

$= \dfrac{{p}_{0}{V}_{0}}{\dfrac{3}{2}{p}_{0}{V}_{0} + 5{p}_{0}{V}_{0}} = \dfrac{2}{13}$

Efficiency $\left(%\right) = \dfrac{2}{13} \times 100 = 15 . 4 %$

questions.q: The pressure versus temperature graph of an ideal gas is shown in the figure below. If the density of gas at point $A$ is ${ρ}_{0}$, then the density of the gas at point $B$ will be
questions.solution:
Given, density of gas at point $A, {ρ}_{A} = {ρ}_{0}$

General equation for an ideal gas

$pV = nRT$

$⇒ pV = \dfrac{m}{M}RT$ [$m \to$mass, $M \to$ molecular mass]

$⇒ p = \dfrac{m}{V} \cdot \dfrac{R}{M} \cdot T$

$⇒ p = ρ\left(\dfrac{R}{M}\right)T . . . \left(i\right)$ [where density $ρ = \dfrac{m}{V}$]

Applying Equation. (i) at point $A$ and $B$, respectively.

$p = {ρ}_{A}\left(\dfrac{R}{M}\right){T}_{0} . . . \left(ii\right)$

$2p = {ρ}_{B}\left(\dfrac{R}{M}\right)3{T}_{0} . . . \left(iii\right)$

From Equations. (ii) and (iii), we get

$\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{{ρ}_{A}}{{ρ}_{B}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ {ρ}_{B} = \dfrac{2}{3}{ρ}_{A} = \dfrac{2}{3}{ρ}_{0}$

Change in internal energy, i.e.
$\begin{gathered}

$\begin{array}{ll}

\end{array}$

$\text\ln \text{G} ⟶ \text{H}$ work done is less than $3 1 {\text{P}}_{0} {\text{V}}_{0}$ i.e., $2 4 {\text{P}}_{0} {\text{V}}_{0}$

A gas can be taken from $A$ to $B$ via two different processes $ACB$ and $ADB$.

When path $ACB$ is used $60J$ of heat flows into the system and $30J$ of work is done by the system. If the path $ADB$ is used then work done by the system is $10J$, the heat flows into the system in the path $ADB$ is:

$⇒ \Delta U = 30J$
For path $ADB$
$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$
As initial and find points are the same, change in internal energy is same in both the cases
$\Delta Q = 30 + 10$
$= 40J$

questions.q: If one mole of an ideal gas at $\left({P}_{1}, {V}_{1}\right)$ is allowed to expand reversibly and isothermally ($A to B$) its pressure is reduced to one-half of the original pressure (see figure). This is followed by a constant volume cooling till its pressure is reduced to one-fourth of the initial value $\left(B \to C\right) .$ Then it is restored to its initial state by a reversible adiabatic compression ($C to A$). The net workdone by the gas is equal to:
questions.solution:
$A - B =$ isothermal process

${W}_{AB} = {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left[\dfrac{2{V}_{1}}{{V}_{1}}\right] = {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left(2\right)$

$B - C \to$ Isochoric process

${W}_{BC} = 0$

$C - A \to$Adiabatic process

${W}_{CA} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} - \dfrac{{P}_{1}}{4} \times 2{V}_{1}}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right]}{1 - \gamma} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}$

${W}_{net} = {W}_{AB} + {W}_{BC} + {W}_{CA}\left\{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} = RT\right\}$

$= {P}_{1}{V}_{1}ln\left(2\right) + 0 + \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1}}{2\left(1 - \gamma\right)}$

${W}_{net} = RT\left[ln\left(2\right) - \dfrac{1}{2\left(\gamma - 1\right)}\right]$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If heat is added to a system, its temperature must increase.

Statement II: If positive work is done by a system in a thermodynamic process, its volume must increase.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
If heat energy is added to a thermodynamic system, one part increases the internal energy and the other part performs some work.

If heat is added to a system, the system can do work without changing its internal energy. Hence, statement 1 is false.

The formula to calculate the work done is given by

$W = ∫ PdV$

From the above equation, it can be concluded that if $W > 0$, i.e., work is done by the system, its volume must increase. Hence, statement II is true.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion A : If $dQ$ and $dW$ represent the heat supplied to the system and the work done on the system respectively. Then according to the first law of thermodynamics $dQ = dU - dW$.

Reason R : First law of thermodynamics is based on law of conservation of energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the option given below :
options: A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.solution:
The first law of thermodynamics is stated as $dQ = dU - dW$. Since $dQ$ is heat supplied to the system and positive thus, $dW$ is work done on the system, i.e., negative work.

We know that the first law of thermodynamics deals with work done, and heat energy supplied or removed from a system. Therefore, it is based on the conservation of energy. The  law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another.

questions.q:
Statement - I : When $\mu$ amount of an ideal gas undergoes adiabatic change from state $\left({P}_{1}, {V}_{1}, {T}_{1}\right)$ to state $\left({P}_{2}, {V}_{2}, {T}_{2}\right)$, then work done is $W = \dfrac{\muR\left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right)}{1 - \gamma}$, where $\gamma = \dfrac{{C}_{P}}{{C}_{V}}$ and R = universal gas constant.

Statement - II : In the above case, when work is done on the gas, the temperature of the gas would rise.
options: Both statement-I and statement-II are true.
Both statement-I and statement-II are false.
Statement-I is true but statement-II is false.
Statement-I is false but statement-II is true.
questions.solution:
The work done in an adiabatic process is given by,

${W}_{adiabatic} = \dfrac{nR\left({T}_{f} - {T}_{i}\right)}{1 - \gamma} \to$ statement I is true.

For adiabatic process $∆ Q = 0$. From the first law of thermodynamics,

$∆ Q = W + \DeltaU$

$0 = W + \DeltaU$

$\DeltaU = - W$

If work is done on the gas, i.e. work is negative

$∴ \DeltaU$ is positive.

$∴$ The temperature will increase. Hence, statement II is also true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : Evaporation has a cooling effect.
Reason (R) : At the surface of liquid, some of the faster upward moving molecules have enough kinetic energy to overcome the attraction from other molecules and escape from the liquid. With these faster molecules the average kinetic energy left behind is reduced.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
The correct option is A Statement 1 and statement 2 both are correct and statement 2 is the correct explanation of statement 1.
When a liquid is placed in an open vessel, its molecules constantly move in different directions with different velocities. Thus, as these molecules are moving at different speeds, they possess different kinetic energies. At any particular temperature, the energies of some surface molecules may be higher so that they can overcome the forces of attraction of the neighboring molecules and can leave the liquid and come above the surface of the liquid. This process is called evaporation. Evaporation is a spontaneous process. It occurs spontaneously at all temperatures. During evaporation, the surface molecules with high kinetic energy leave the liquid and come above the surface of the liquid. The molecules remaining in the liquid state have lesser energy and hence the temperature reduces. This is the reason why evaporation causes cooling. Therefore, statement 1 and 2 both are correct and statement 2 is the correct explanation of statement 1.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Heat is given to an ideal gas in an isothermal process.

A. Internal energy of the gas will decrease.

B. Internal energy of the gas will increase.

C. Internal energy of the gas will not change.

D. The gas will do positive work.

E. The gas will do negative work.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
From the first law of thermodynamics, heat supplied to the system $Q$, change in internal energy of the system $∆ U$ and work done by the system $W$ are related as:

$Q = ∆ U + W$

Since the process is isothermal, the temperature of the system is constant and therefore $∆ U = 0$ (i.e., internal energy is constant). 

$⇒ Q = W$

As heat is supplied to the system, $Q$ is positive and therefore $W$ is positive i.e., gas will do positive work.

Hence, correct options are C and D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the following
List - Iamp; List - II
i) Isothermal processamp; a) 0
ii) Isobaric processamp; b) $\frac{1}{\gamma-1}\left[$P_2 V_2-P_1 V_1\right]
iii) Isochoric processamp; c) \mu RT \ln $\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$
iv) Adiabatic processamp; d) P $\left(V_2-V_1\right)
$ The correct answer is
questions.solution:
Work done in any quasi-static process \(=W=\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P d V\). Evaluate this for each process.
i) Isothermal process (\($\mathrm{T}=$ constant).
Use ideal gas: \(P V=n R T\) (constant \(T \Rightarrow n R T=\) constant).
\(W=\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P d V=\int_{V_1}^{V_2} $\frac{n R T}{V}$d V=n R T \ln $\frac{V_2}{V_1}$
So isothermal \(\Rightarrow\) match (c).
ii) Isobaric process (\($\mathrm{P}=$ constant).
If pressure is constant,
\(W=\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P d V=P$\left(V_2-V_1\right)\)
So isobaric \(\Rightarrow\) match (d).
iii) Isochoric process (\($\mathrm{V}=$constant).
If volume is constant \(d V=0\), therefore
\(W=\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P d V=0\)
So isochoric \(\Rightarrow\) match (a).
iv) Adiabatic (reversible) process.$ For adiabatic reversible: \(P V^\gamma=$ constant. Let \(P V^$\gamma=$K\). Then
\(W=\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P d V=K \int_{V_1}^{V_2} V^{-$\gamma$} d V=$\frac{K}{1-\gamma}\left(V_2^{1-$\gamma$}-V_1^{1-$\gamma$}\right)\)
Using \(K=P_1 V_1^$\gamma=$P_2 V_2^$\gamma$ and simplifying gives the standard form
\(W=$\frac{P_1 V_1-P_2 V_2}{\gamma-1} .$
So adiabatic \(\Rightarrow\) match (b).
Final matching:
i - c, ii \(-d\), iii \(-a\), iv \(-b\).

questions.q:
Match of the following.
$

Column I		Column II

$\begin{array}{ll}
A. Ratio of $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta U} in$an isobaric

process
\end{array}$		1. \frac{T_1}{\left(T_1-T_2\right)}

$\begin{array}{ll}
B. Ratio of $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta W} in$an isobaric

process
\end{array}$		2. \frac{T_2}{\left(T_1-T_2\right)}

\begin{array}{l}
C. Coefficient$ of $performance

of a refrigerator
\end{array}		3. \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}

\begin{array}{l}
D. Coefficient of performance

of a heat pump
\end{array}		4. \gamma



Codes
\begin{array}{llll}A & B & C & D\end{array}$
questions.solution:
We know that, at constant volume, Heat supplied, $\Delta Q_1=\Delta U=C_V \Delta T$
At constant pressure, heat supplied,
$\Delta Q=C_p \Delta T=\Delta U+\Delta W$
Ratio of heat capacity at constant pressure to constant volume is
$\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_V}$
Now, $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta U}=\frac{C_p \Delta T}{C_V \Delta T}=\frac{C_p}{C_V}=\gamma$
Now, $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta W}=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta Q-\Delta U} =\frac{C_p \Delta T}{C_p \Delta T-C_V \Delta T} \begin{aligned}
& =\frac{C_p}{C_p-C_V}=\frac{C_p}{C_V\left(\frac{C_p}{C_V}-1\right)} \\
& =\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}
\end{aligned}$
For refrigerator, coefficient of performance,
$\begin{aligned}
\beta & =\frac{Q_2}{W}=\frac{\text{ Heat absorbed from food stuff }}{\text{ Electrical work done }} \\
\therefore \quad \beta & =\frac{Q_2}{Q_1-Q_2}
\end{aligned}$
Coefficient of heat pump $=\frac{\text{ Heat released }}{\text{ Electrical work }}$
i.e. $\quad \alpha=\frac{Q_1}{W}=\frac{Q_1}{Q_1-Q_2}$
We know that, $\frac{Q_1}{Q_2}=\frac{T_1}{T_2}$
So, we get, $\beta=\frac{Q_2}{Q_1-Q_2}=\frac{\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}}{1-\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}} =\frac{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}{1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}}=\frac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$
and $\alpha=\frac{Q_1}{Q_1-Q_2} =\frac{\frac{Q_1}{Q_2}}{\frac{Q_1}{Q_2}-1}=\frac{\frac{T_1}{T_2}}{\frac{T_1}{T_2}-1} =\frac{T_1}{T_1-T_2}$
Hence, we get the best match as given by $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow 4, \mathrm{ B} \rightarrow 3, \mathrm{C} \rightarrow 2$ and $\mathrm{D} \rightarrow 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is taken through a cycle $A B C D A$ as shown in the $p$-V diagram. Column II gives the characteristics involved in the cycle. Match them with each of the processes given in Column I.
questions.solution:
Internal energy $\propto T \propto p V$
This is because
$U=\frac{n f}{2} R T=\frac{f}{2} p V$
Here, $n=$ number of moles
$f=$ degree of freedom
If the product $p V$ increases, then internal energy will increase and if product decreases, the internal energy will decrease.
Further, work is done on the gas, if volume of gas decreases. For heat exchange.
$Q=W+\Delta U$
Work done is area under $p-V$ graph. If volume increases work done by gas is positive and if volume decreases work done by gas is negative. Further $\Delta U$ is positive if product of $p V$ is increasing and $N U$ is negative, if product of $p V$ is decreasing. If heat is taken by the gas $Q$ is positive and if heat is lost by the gas $Q$ is negative.
Keeping the above points in mind the answer to this question is as under.
(A) $\rightarrow(\mathrm{p}, \mathrm{r}, \mathrm{t})$
(B) $\rightarrow(\mathrm{p}, \mathrm{r})$
(C) $\rightarrow$ (q, s)
(D) $\rightarrow(\mathrm{r}, \mathrm{t})$
Analysis of Question
(i) Calculation wise, question is slightly lengthy. Otherwise question is theory based and simple.
(ii) In process $D A$,
$\begin{array}{rlrl} & & p_A V_A & =p_D V_D \\ \therefore & & T_A & =T_D \\ \text{ or } & \Delta U & =0\end{array}$
Further, volume of gas is decreasing. Therefore, work is done on the gas or work done by gas is negative. Therefore, $Q is negative or heat is lost.
(iii) This question covers almost all the concepts of first law of thermodynamics.$

questions.q:
Answer the following by appropriately matching the lists based on the information given in the paragraph.
In a thermodynamics process on an ideal monatomic gas, the infinitesimal heat absorbed by the gas is given by $T\DeltaX,$ where $T$ is temperature of the system and $\DeltaX$ is the infinitesimal change in a thermodynamic quantity $X$ of the system. For a mole of monatomic ideal gas $X = \dfrac{3}{2}Rln\left(\dfrac{T}{{T}_{A}}\right) + Rln\left(\dfrac{V}{{V}_{A}}\right) .$ Here, $R$ is gas constant, $V$ is volume of gas, ${T}_{A}$ and ${V}_{A}$ are constants.
The List-I below gives some quantities involved in a process and List-II gives some possible values of these quantities.
 

 List I List II
$( a )$Work done by the system in process $1 \to 2 \to 3$$( p )$$\dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0}ln2$
$( b )$Change in internal energy in process $1 \to 2 \to 3$$( q )$$\dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0}$
$( c )$Heat absorbed by the system in process $1 \to 2 \to 3$$( r )$$R{T}_{0}$
$( d )$Heat absorbed by the system in process $1 \to 2$$( s )$$\dfrac{4}{3}R{T}_{0}$
  $( t )$$\dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0}\left(3 + ln2\right)$
  $( u )$$\dfrac{5}{6}R{T}_{0}$

If the process carried out on one mole of monatomic ideal gas is as shown in figure in the $T$ - $V$ -diagram with ${P}_{0}{V}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0},$ the correct match is,
options: $a - q, b - r, c - p, d - u$
$a - s, b - r, c - q, d - t$
$a - q, b - r, c - s, d - u$
$a - p, b - r, c - t, d - p$
questions.solution:
$1$ - $2$ process is isothermal and $2$ - $3$ process is isochoric.
$\left(a\right){W}_{1 \to 2} = nRTln\dfrac{{V}_{f}}{{F}_{i}} = 1 \times R\dfrac{{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ \dfrac{{V}_{2}}{{V}_{1}} = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ \dfrac{2{V}_{0}}{{V}_{0}} = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2$
${W}_{2 \to 3} = 0$ (isochoric process)
${W}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} = {W}_{1 \to 2} + {W}_{2 \to 3} = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2\left(a \to P\right)$
$\left(b\right) ∆ U = \dfrac{f}{2}nR\left({T}_{f} - {T}_{i}\right)$
$∆ {U}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} = \dfrac{3}{2}\left[1 \times R\left({T}_{0} - \dfrac{{T}_{0}}{3}\right)\right]$
$\begin{cases}= R{T}_{0} & \left(b \to R\right)\end{cases}$
$\left(c\right){Q}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} = ∆ {U}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} + {W}_{1 \to 2 \to 3}$ (First law of thermodynamics)
$= R{T}_{0} + \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2$
$\begin{cases}= \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}\left[3 + ln ⁡ 2\right] & \left(c \to t\right)\end{cases}$
$\left(d\right){Q}_{1 \to 2} = ∆ {U}_{1 \to 2} + {W}_{1 \to 2}$
$\begin{cases}= 0 + \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2 = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2 & \left(d \to p\right)\end{cases}$

$\left(a\right){W}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} = {W}_{1 \to 2} + {W}_{2 \to 3}$

questions.q:
List I describes thermodynamic processes in four different systems. List II gives the magnitudes (either exactly or as a close approximation) of possible changes in the internal energy of the system due to the process.

  List-I   List-II
(I) ${10}^{- 3}kg$ of water $100 ° C$ is converted to steam at the same temperature, at a pressure of ${10}^{5}Pa$. The volume of the system changes from ${10}^{- 6}{m}^{3}$ to ${10}^{- 3}{m}^{3}$ in the process. Latent heat of water $= 2250kJ{kg}^{- 1}$ (P) $2kJ$
(II) $0 . 2$ moles of a rigid diatomic ideal gas with volume $V$ at temperature $500K$ undergoes an isobaric expansion to volume $3V$. Assume $8 . 0J{mol}^{– 1}{K}^{– 1}$ (Q) $7kJ$
(III) One mole of a monoatomic ideal gas is compressed adiabatically from volume $V = \dfrac{1}{3}{m}^{3}$ and pressure $2kPa$ to volume $\dfrac{V}{8}$. (R) $4kJ$
(IV) Three moles of a diatomic ideal gas whose molecules can vibrate, is given $9kJ$ of heat and undergoes isobaric expansion. (S) $5kJ$
    (T) $3kJ$

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: $I \to T, II \to R, III \to S, IV \to Q$
$I \to S, II \to P, III \to T, IV \to P$
$I \to P, II \to R, III \to T, IV \to Q$
$I \to Q, II \to R, III \to S, IV \to T$
questions.solution:
(I)

According to the first law of thermodynamics,

$∆ Q = ∆ U + W ⇒ ∆ U = ∆ Q - W$

$⇒ U = ML - P\DeltaV$

$= {10}^{- 3} \times 2250 - {10}^{2}kP \times \left({10}^{- 3} - {10}^{- 6}\right){m}^{3}$

$= 2 . 25kJ - 0 . 1kJ$

$= 2 . 15kJ$

Therefore, I-P

(II)

For isobaric process,

$\dfrac{{V}_{1}}{{V}_{2}} = \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} ⇒ {T}_{2} = 3 \times 500 = 1500K$

Now the change in the internal energy will be,

$∆ U = n{C}_{V} ∆ T = 0 . 2 \times \dfrac{5}{2} \times 8 \times 1000 = 4kJ$

Therefore, II-R

(III) 

For adiabatic expansion of monoatomic gas $\left(\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}\right)$

${P}_{1}{V}_{1}^{\gamma} = {P}_{2}{V}_{2}^{\gamma} ⇒ \left(2kPa\right) \times {V}_{0}^{\dfrac{5}{3}} = {P}_{2} \times \left(\dfrac{{V}_{0}}{8}\right)\dfrac{5}{3}$

$⇒ {P}_{2} = 64kPa$

Now the change in the internal energy will be,

$\DeltaU = n{C}_{v}\DeltaT$

$= \dfrac{3nR\DeltaT}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\left({P}_{2}{V}_{2} - {P}_{1}{V}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(64 \times \dfrac{1}{3 \times 8} - 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

$= \dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 3kJ$

Therefore, III-T

(IV)

For diatomic gas whose molecules vibrate,

${C}_{V} = \dfrac{6}{2}R$ and ${C}_{P} = \dfrac{8}{2}R$

$⇒ \DeltaU = n{C}_{V}\DeltaT = 3nR\DeltaT$

$\DeltaQ = n{C}_{p}\DeltaT = 4nR\DeltaT$

$\dfrac{\DeltaU}{\DeltaQ} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$\DeltaU = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 9 = 6 . 75 ≃ 7kJ$

Therefore, IV-Q

questions.q:
Match List I with List II :

  List I   List II
A Isothermal Process I Work done by the gas decreases internal energy
B Adiabatic Process II No change in internal energy
C Isochoric Process III The heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work
D Isobaric Process IV No work is done on or by the gas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
(A) Change in internal energy is expressed as$∆ U = n{C}_{v} ∆ T$, here, $∆ T$ is change in temperature.

Since, in an isothermal process temperature remains constant, thus, $∆ U = 0$

$A \to II$

(B) In an adiabatic process, heat transfer, $Q = 0$.

So, from first law of thermodynamics, 

$Q = ∆ U + W$

$∆ U = - W$

Since, work done by gas is positive, thus, $∆ U$ is negative

$B \to I$

(C) In an isochoric process, volume remains constant, so work done by or on the gas $W = P ∆ V = 0$

$C \to IV$

(D) In an isobaric process, pressure remains constant, so work done$W = P ∆ V \ne 0$ and change in internal energy $∆ U = n{C}_{v} ∆ T \ne 0$

Thus, heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly do work.

$D \to III$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Read the following statements regarding thermodynamic processes:

Statement I: If equal heat is supplied to two gases at the same constant pressure and their internal energy increases by the same amount, a piston with double the radius will undergo one-fourth the displacement.
Statement II: During the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the heat supplied is entirely converted into work done by the gas.
Statement III: For two different ideal gases expanding at the same constant pressure, if the same amount of heat is supplied, the work done is independent of the atomicity of the gases.
Statement IV: The work done by a gas displacing a piston at constant pressure is directly proportional to the radius of the piston for a given displacement.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct: From the First Law of Thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W$. If $Q$ and $\Delta U$ are the same, the work done $W$ is the same. Work done at constant pressure is $W = P \Delta V = P(\pi r^2)x$. For $W$ and $P$ to be constant, $r^2 x$ must be constant. If $r$ is doubled, $r^2$ becomes four times, so $x$ must become one-fourth.

Statement II is correct: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas, the change in internal energy $\Delta U = 0$. Therefore, $Q = W$, meaning all supplied heat is converted into work.

Statement III is incorrect: At constant pressure, $W = nR\Delta T$ and $Q = nC_p\Delta T$. The ratio $\dfrac{W}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{C_p}$. Since molar heat capacity at constant pressure ($C_p$) depends on the atomicity of the gas, the work done for a given amount of heat will vary for gases with different atomicity.

Statement IV is incorrect: Work done $W = P(\pi r^2)x$. For a given displacement $x$ and constant pressure $P$, the work done is directly proportional to the square of the radius ($r^2$), not the radius ($r$).

Therefore, exactly two statements (I and II) are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If an ideal gas undergoes a thermodynamic process where its volume is directly proportional to the square of its absolute temperature ($V \propto T^2$), its pressure will decrease as it expands.

Reason (R): In this process, the pressure of the gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its volume ($P \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is not correct.
Assertion (A) is not correct but Reason (R) is correct.
questions.solution:
From the Assertion, the process follows the relation $V \propto T^2$.

This can be rewritten as $T \propto V^{1/2}$.

According to the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, which implies $P \propto \dfrac{T}{V}$.

Substituting the relation for $T$ into the pressure proportionality:
$P \propto \dfrac{V^{1/2}}{V}$

$P \propto V^{-1/2} \implies P \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$

This shows that the Reason (R) is a correct statement.

Because $P \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$, an increase in volume $V$ (expansion) will lead to a decrease in pressure $P$. Thus, the Assertion (A) is also correct.

Since the inverse relationship between pressure and the square root of volume is the exact mathematical cause for the pressure decrease during expansion, Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two ideal gases $A$ and $B$ are contained in separate horizontal cylinders fitted with movable pistons. The ratio of the pressures of the gases is $P_A : P_B = 2 : 1$, and the ratio of the radii of their pistons is $r_A : r_B = 1 : 2$. When an equal amount of heat is supplied to both systems, their internal energies increase by the same amount. What is the ratio of the displacements of the pistons, $x_A : x_B$?
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W$.

Given that $Q_A = Q_B$ and $\Delta U_A = \Delta U_B$, the work done by both gases must be equal:
$W_A = W_B$

The work done by a gas expanding at constant pressure is $W = P \Delta V$. For a cylinder with piston radius $r$ and displacement $x$, the change in volume is $\Delta V = \pi r^2 x$.

Thus, $P_A (\pi r_A^2 x_A) = P_B (\pi r_B^2 x_B)$

Rearranging for the ratio of displacements:
$\dfrac{x_A}{x_B} = \dfrac{P_B}{P_A} \times \left(\dfrac{r_B}{r_A}\right)^2$

Substituting the given ratios $\dfrac{P_A}{P_B} = \dfrac{2}{1}$ and $\dfrac{r_A}{r_B} = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$\dfrac{x_A}{x_B} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{2}{1}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 = \dfrac{2}{1}$

Therefore, the ratio of the displacements is $2 : 1$.

Answer: $2 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the molar heat capacity ($C$) of an ideal gas for different thermodynamic processes.

List-I (Process)List-II (Molar heat capacity)
A. IsothermalI. Zero
B. AdiabaticII. Infinity
C. IsobaricIII. $C_p$
D. IsochoricIV. $C_v$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Molar heat capacity is defined as $C = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{n \Delta T}$.

For an isothermal process, the temperature is constant ($\Delta T = 0$), so $C \to \infty$.

For an adiabatic process, there is no heat exchange ($\Delta Q = 0$), so $C = 0$.

For an isobaric process, the heat capacity at constant pressure is $C_p$.

For an isochoric process, the heat capacity at constant volume is $C_v$.

Thus, the correct matching is A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

Answer: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical cylinders, each fitted with a movable piston of the same radius, contain equal number of moles of two different ideal gases. Gas $A$ is monatomic and Gas $B$ is diatomic. Both gases are heated at constant pressure by supplying the same amount of heat $Q$. If the pistons move outward without friction, what is the ratio of the displacement of the piston for Gas $A$ to that for Gas $B$ ($x_A : x_B$)?
questions.solution:
For an isobaric process, the heat supplied is $Q = n C_p \Delta T$ and the work done by the gas is $W = n R \Delta T$.

From these, the work done can be expressed in terms of heat supplied as:
$W = Q \left(\dfrac{R}{C_p}\right)$

For the monatomic gas $A$, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure is $C_{p,A} = \dfrac{5}{2}R$.
Thus, $W_A = Q \left(\dfrac{R}{\dfrac{5}{2}R}\right) = \dfrac{2Q}{5}$

For the diatomic gas $B$, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure is $C_{p,B} = \dfrac{7}{2}R$.
Thus, $W_B = Q \left(\dfrac{R}{\dfrac{7}{2}R}\right) = \dfrac{2Q}{7}$

The work done by the gas in moving the piston by distance $x$ is $W = P \Delta V = P (\pi r^2) x$. Since the pressure $P$ and radius $r$ are identical for both cylinders, the displacement $x$ is directly proportional to the work done $W$.

Therefore, the ratio of displacements is:
$\dfrac{x_A}{x_B} = \dfrac{W_A}{W_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2Q}{5}}{\dfrac{2Q}{7}} = \dfrac{7}{5}$

Answer: $7 : 5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Heat is supplied to a monoatomic ideal gas at a constant rate of $150\text{ W}$. If the gas expands isobarically, the rate at which the gas does work is :
questions.solution:
For a monoatomic ideal gas undergoing an isobaric process, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure is $C_p = \dfrac{5}{2}R$.

The heat supplied is given by $dQ = nC_pdT = \dfrac{5}{2}nRdT$.

The work done by the gas during expansion is $dW = pdV = nRdT$.

Taking the ratio of work done to heat supplied:
$\dfrac{dW}{dQ} = \dfrac{nRdT}{\dfrac{5}{2}nRdT} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

Differentiating with respect to time $t$, we get the relationship between their rates:
$\dfrac{dW}{dt} = \dfrac{2}{5} \dfrac{dQ}{dt}$

Given that the rate of heat supplied is $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 150\text{ W}$:
$\dfrac{dW}{dt} = \dfrac{2}{5} \times 150\text{ W} = 60\text{ W}$

Answer: $60\text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): On a $P-V$ diagram, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve for a given ideal gas.
Reason (R): The magnitude of the slope of the isothermal curve is $\gamma$ (ratio of specific heats) times the magnitude of the slope of the adiabatic curve at any given point.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
The slope of an isothermal process on a $P-V$ diagram is given by $\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\dfrac{P}{V}$.

The slope of an adiabatic process is given by $\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\gamma \dfrac{P}{V}$.

Since $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v} > 1$ for all ideal gases, the magnitude of the adiabatic slope is $\gamma$ times the magnitude of the isothermal slope. This makes the adiabatic curve steeper than the isothermal curve.

Therefore, the Assertion is correct, but the Reason is incorrect because it incorrectly states that the isothermal slope is $\gamma$ times the adiabatic slope.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas expands in a cylinder, pushing a piston outward at a constant speed of $0.2\text{ m/s}$ against a constant external force of $400\text{ N}$. If heat is being supplied to the gas at a rate of $120\text{ W}$, what is the rate of increase of the internal energy of the gas?
questions.solution:
The rate at which work is done by the gas (mechanical power) is given by the product of force and velocity:

$\dfrac{dW}{dt} = F \times v = 400 \times 0.2 = 80\text{ W}$

Since the gas expands, work is done by the system, so $\dfrac{dW}{dt} = +80\text{ W}$.

The rate of heat supplied to the gas is $\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 120\text{ W}$.

According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dU}{dt} + \dfrac{dW}{dt}$

Substituting the known values:

$120 = \dfrac{dU}{dt} + 80$

$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 120 - 80 = 40\text{ W}$

The internal energy of the gas increases at a rate of $40\text{ W}$.

Answer: $40\text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two moles of an ideal gas undergo a cyclic process $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$ represented on a Pressure-Temperature ($P-T$) diagram. The cycle forms a right-angled triangle with vertices at $A(300 \text{ K}, 1 \text{ atm})$, $B(600 \text{ K}, 1 \text{ atm})$, and $C(300 \text{ K}, 0.5 \text{ atm})$. The work done by the gas during the isobaric segment of the cycle is:
questions.solution:
The isobaric (constant pressure) segment of the cycle is the process $A \rightarrow B$, where the pressure remains constant at $1 \text{ atm}$.

During this process, the temperature increases from $T_A = 300 \text{ K}$ to $T_B = 600 \text{ K}$.

The work done by an ideal gas during an isobaric process is given by:
$W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$

Given $n = 2$ moles, the change in temperature is $\Delta T = 600 \text{ K} - 300 \text{ K} = 300 \text{ K}$.

Substituting the values:
$W = 2 \times R \times 300 = 600 R$

Calculating the area of the triangle on the $P-T$ graph ($75$) does not give the work done, and using $n=1$ gives the incorrect value of $300 R$.

Answer: $600 R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is taken from state 1 to state 2 through a process represented by a straight line on a Pressure (P) versus Volume (V) diagram. The coordinates $(V, P)$ of state 1 are $(10 \text{ L}, 20 \text{ kPa})$ and of state 2 are $(30 \text{ L}, 60 \text{ kPa})$. If the heat supplied to the gas during this process is $2000 \text{ J}$, what is the change in its internal energy?
questions.solution:
The work done by the gas is the area under the P-V graph from state 1 to state 2. Since the process is represented by a straight line, the area under the curve forms a trapezium.

Work done, $\Delta W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (P_1 + P_2) \times (V_2 - V_1)$

Given $P_1 = 20 \text{ kPa}$, $P_2 = 60 \text{ kPa}$, $V_1 = 10 \text{ L}$, and $V_2 = 30 \text{ L}$.

$\Delta W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (20 + 60) \times 10^3 \text{ Pa} \times (30 - 10) \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$

$\Delta W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 20 \text{ J} = 800 \text{ J}$

According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$

Given the heat supplied to the system, $\Delta Q = 2000 \text{ J}$.

$2000 \text{ J} = \Delta U + 800 \text{ J}$

$\Delta U = 1200 \text{ J}$

Answer: $1200 \text{ J}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In an isobaric expansion of an ideal gas, the heat supplied to the gas is always less than the work done by the gas.

Reason (R): During an isobaric expansion, the temperature of the ideal gas increases, leading to an increase in its internal energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
In an isobaric process, pressure is constant. For an ideal gas, $V \propto T$ at constant pressure. During expansion, volume increases, so temperature must increase. This leads to an increase in internal energy ($\Delta U > 0$). Thus, the Reason is correct.

According to the first law of thermodynamics, $Q = W + \Delta U$. Since $\Delta U$ is positive during an isobaric expansion, the heat supplied ($Q$) must be greater than the work done ($W$). The Assertion states that heat supplied is less than work done, which is incorrect.

Therefore, (A) is not correct but (R) is correct.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is compressed from an initial volume $V_{0}$ to a final volume $\dfrac{V_{0}}{2}$ starting from the same initial state $(P_{0}, V_{0})$. The compression is carried out along two different paths, represented by curves A and B on a P-V diagram. If curve A lies above curve B (i.e., curve A ends at a higher pressure than curve B), which of the following correctly identifies the two processes?
options: Curve A is adiabatic and curve B is isothermal
Curve A is isothermal and curve B is adiabatic
Both curves represent isothermal processes at different temperatures
Both curves represent adiabatic processes for different gases
questions.solution:
The slope of a P-V curve is given by $\dfrac{dP}{dV}$.

For an isothermal process, the slope is $-\dfrac{P}{V}$.

For an adiabatic process, the slope is $-\gamma\dfrac{P}{V}$.

Since $\gamma > 1$, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve.

During compression, the volume decreases. Starting from the same initial state, the steeper adiabatic curve will rise more rapidly than the isothermal curve. Therefore, the adiabatic curve will lie above the isothermal curve on the P-V diagram, reaching a higher final pressure.

Since curve A ends at a higher pressure than curve B, curve A represents the adiabatic process and curve B represents the isothermal process.

Answer: Curve A is adiabatic and curve B is isothermal

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two vertical cylinders are placed in a vacuum chamber and contain ideal gases. They are fitted with heavy, frictionless movable pistons. The piston of cylinder $A$ has mass $m$ and radius $r$, while the piston of cylinder $B$ has mass $2m$ and radius $2r$. Equal amounts of heat are supplied to both gases, and they undergo an expansion such that the change in their internal energies is the same. The ratio of the upward displacement of piston $A$ to that of piston $B$ ($x_A : x_B$) is:
questions.solution:
From the First Law of Thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W$.

Since $Q_A = Q_B$ and $\Delta U_A = \Delta U_B$, the work done by both gases must be equal ($W_A = W_B$).

In a vacuum chamber, the external atmospheric pressure is zero. The pressure of the gas is purely due to the weight of the piston: $P = \dfrac{mg}{\pi r^2}$.

The work done by the gas during an upward displacement $x$ is $W = P \Delta V = \left(\dfrac{mg}{\pi r^2}\right) (\pi r^2 x) = mgx$.

Notice that the work done is simply the change in gravitational potential energy of the piston, which is independent of the piston's radius.

Equating the work done for both cylinders:
$m_A g x_A = m_B g x_B$
$m g x_A = (2m) g x_B$
$\dfrac{x_A}{x_B} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

The ratio of their displacements is $2 : 1$.

Answer: $2 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One mole of an ideal diatomic gas undergoes a thermodynamic process described by the equation $PT = \text{constant}$, where $P$ is pressure and $T$ is absolute temperature. The molar heat capacity of the gas for this process is:
questions.solution:
The given process equation is $PT = \text{constant}$.

From the ideal gas equation, $T = \dfrac{PV}{nR}$. Substituting this into the process equation gives:
$P\left(\dfrac{PV}{nR}\right) = \text{constant}$
$P^2V = \text{constant}'$
$P V^{1/2} = \text{constant}''$

Comparing this with the standard polytropic process equation $PV^x = \text{constant}$, we get the polytropic index $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

The molar heat capacity for a polytropic process is given by:
$C = C_v + \dfrac{R}{1-x}$

For a diatomic gas, the molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_v = \dfrac{5}{2}R$.

Substituting the values of $C_v$ and $x$:
$C = \dfrac{5}{2}R + \dfrac{R}{1 - 1/2}$
$C = \dfrac{5}{2}R + \dfrac{R}{1/2}$
$C = \dfrac{5}{2}R + 2R = \dfrac{9}{2}R$.

Answer: $\dfrac{9}{2}R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas of $n$ moles is taken from state 1 to state 2. On a pressure-temperature ($P-T$) diagram, this process is represented by a straight line passing through the origin. If the temperature of the gas changes from $T_1$ to $T_2$, the work done by the gas is:
questions.solution:
According to the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, which can be rearranged as $P = \left(\dfrac{nR}{V}\right)T$.

The process is given as a straight line passing through the origin on the $P-T$ diagram. The equation of such a line is $P = kT$, where $k$ is a constant slope.

Comparing the two equations, we get $\dfrac{nR}{V} = k$. Since $n$, $R$, and $k$ are constants, the volume $V$ must also be constant.

A process where the volume remains constant is an isochoric process ($\Delta V = 0$).

The work done by a gas is given by $W = \int P \, dV$. Since there is no change in volume, the work done by the gas is zero.

Answer: Zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas undergoes a thermodynamic process in which its pressure is directly proportional to its volume ($P \propto V$). Which of the following correctly describes the shape of the graph showing the variation of its absolute temperature ($T$) on the y-axis with volume ($V$) on the x-axis?
options: A straight line passing through the origin
A parabola opening towards the temperature axis
A parabola opening towards the volume axis
questions.solution:
Given that pressure is directly proportional to volume, we can write $P = kV$, where $k$ is a positive constant.

From the ideal gas equation, we have $PV = nRT$.

Substituting $P = kV$ into the ideal gas equation gives:
$(kV)V = nRT$
$kV^2 = nRT$
$T = \left(\dfrac{k}{nR}\right)V^2$

This equation is of the form $y = cx^2$, which represents a parabola opening upwards (towards the y-axis, which is the temperature axis).

Therefore, the graph of $T$ versus $V$ is a parabola opening towards the temperature axis.

Answer: A parabola opening towards the temperature axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas undergoes a clockwise cyclic process consisting of three steps. The states of the gas at the vertices of the cycle on a $P-V$ diagram are $(V_0, 2P_0)$, $(3V_0, 2P_0)$, and $(V_0, P_0)$. What is the ratio of the work done by the gas during the isobaric expansion segment to the net work done by the gas in the entire cycle?
questions.solution:
The cyclic process forms a right-angled triangle on the $P-V$ diagram.

The isobaric expansion occurs at a constant pressure of $2P_0$ from volume $V_0$ to $3V_0$.
Work done during this expansion, $W_{exp} = P \Delta V = 2P_0(3V_0 - V_0) = 4P_0V_0$.

The net work done in the clockwise cycle is the area of the triangle enclosed on the $P-V$ diagram.
Base of the triangle (change in volume) = $3V_0 - V_0 = 2V_0$.
Height of the triangle (change in pressure) = $2P_0 - P_0 = P_0$.
Net work, $W_{net} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2V_0 \times P_0 = P_0V_0$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{W_{exp}}{W_{net}} = \dfrac{4P_0V_0}{P_0V_0} = 4$.

Answer: $4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The heat supplied ($Q$) to a thermodynamic system and the work done ($W$) by the system are plotted against time ($t$). Both plots are straight lines passing through the origin. If the $Q$ versus $t$ line passes through the coordinates ($4\text{ s}, 240\text{ J}$) and the $W$ versus $t$ line passes through ($4\text{ s}, 80\text{ J}$), what is the rate of change of internal energy of the system?
questions.solution:
The rate of heat supplied is the slope of the $Q$ versus $t$ graph. Since it is a straight line passing through the origin $(0, 0)$ and the point ($4\text{ s}, 240\text{ J}$):
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{240\text{ J} - 0}{4\text{ s} - 0} = 60\text{ J/s} = 60\text{ W}$

Similarly, the rate of work done is the slope of the $W$ versus $t$ graph, passing through the origin and ($4\text{ s}, 80\text{ J}$):
$\dfrac{dW}{dt} = \dfrac{80\text{ J} - 0}{4\text{ s} - 0} = 20\text{ J/s} = 20\text{ W}$

According to the first law of thermodynamics in rate form:
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dU}{dt} + \dfrac{dW}{dt}$

Substituting the calculated rates:
$60 = \dfrac{dU}{dt} + 20$

$\dfrac{dU}{dt} = 60 - 20 = 40\text{ W}$

The rate of change of internal energy is $40\text{ W}$.

Answer: $40\text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas is taken through a cyclic process $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$. The process $A \rightarrow B$ is an isobaric expansion, $B \rightarrow C$ is a linear process on the $P-V$ indicator diagram, and $C \rightarrow A$ is an isochoric process. The coordinates of the states are $A (2 \text{ L}, 400 \text{ kPa})$, $B (5 \text{ L}, 400 \text{ kPa})$, and $C (2 \text{ L}, P_C)$. If the net work done by the gas in the cycle is $-450 \text{ J}$, what is the value of the pressure $P_C$?
questions.solution:
The net work done in the cyclic process is the sum of the work done in each individual process:
$W_{\text{net}} = W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CA}$

1) Process $A \rightarrow B$ is an isobaric expansion at $P = 400 \text{ kPa}$:
$W_{AB} = P \Delta V = 400 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa} \times (5 - 2) \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3 = 1200 \text{ J}$

2) Process $B \rightarrow C$ is a linear process from $V = 5 \text{ L}$ to $V = 2 \text{ L}$:
The work done is the area under the $P-V$ graph (a trapezium):
$W_{BC} = \dfrac{1}{2} (P_B + P_C) (V_C - V_B)$
$W_{BC} = \dfrac{1}{2} (400 + P_C) \times 10^3 \times (2 - 5) \times 10^{-3} = -1.5 (400 + P_C) \text{ J}$

3) Process $C \rightarrow A$ is isochoric ($\Delta V = 0$):
$W_{CA} = 0 \text{ J}$

Equating the sum to the given net work of $-450 \text{ J}$:
$1200 - 1.5(400 + P_C) + 0 = -450$
$1200 - 600 - 1.5 P_C = -450$
$600 - 1.5 P_C = -450$
$1.5 P_C = 1050$
$P_C = 700 \text{ kPa}$

Answer: $700 \text{ kPa}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas expands from an initial volume $V$ to a final volume $2V$ through three different processes starting from the exact same initial state. The processes are isobaric, isothermal, and adiabatic. Let $W_{1}$, $W_{2}$, and $W_{3}$ be the magnitudes of the work done by the gas in the isobaric, isothermal, and adiabatic processes respectively. Which of the following correctly represents the relationship between the work done in these processes?
questions.solution:
The magnitude of work done by a gas during expansion is equal to the area under the P-V curve for that process.

Starting from the same initial state $(P, V)$ and expanding to the same final volume $2V$:

In an isobaric process, the pressure remains constant, so its P-V curve is a horizontal line.

In an isothermal process, the pressure decreases as volume increases. Its curve falls below the isobaric line.

In an adiabatic process, the pressure decreases more rapidly than in an isothermal process because its curve is steeper (slope is $\gamma$ times the isothermal slope). Its curve falls below the isothermal curve.

Therefore, the area under the curves follows the order: Area(isobaric) > Area(isothermal) > Area(adiabatic).

This means the work done follows the sequence: $W_{1} > W_{2} > W_{3}$.

Answer: $W_{1} > W_{2} > W_{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An ideal gas undergoes a cyclic process A $\rightarrow$ B $\rightarrow$ C $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ A, which forms a rectangle on a Pressure (P) versus Volume (V) diagram. The sides AB and CD are parallel to the volume axis, while BC and DA are parallel to the pressure axis. The volume of the gas increases during the process A $\rightarrow$ B.

Match List-I with List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Process A $\rightarrow$ B(I) Positive work
(B) Process B $\rightarrow$ C(II) Negative work
(C) Process C $\rightarrow$ D(III) Zero work
(D) Net cycle A $\rightarrow$ B $\rightarrow$ C $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ A

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
In a P-V diagram, the work done by a gas is the area under the process curve on the volume axis.

For the process A $\rightarrow$ B, the line is parallel to the volume axis (isobaric) and the volume increases. Since it is an expansion, the work done is positive.

For the process B $\rightarrow$ C, the line is parallel to the pressure axis (isochoric). The volume is constant ($\Delta V = 0$), so the work done is zero.

For the process C $\rightarrow$ D, the process is isobaric and the volume decreases to return to the initial volume coordinate. Since it is a compression, the work done is negative.

The net work done in a cyclic process is the area enclosed by the cycle on the P-V diagram. Since the expansion A $\rightarrow$ B occurs at a higher pressure than the compression C $\rightarrow$ D, the cycle is clockwise and the net work done by the gas is positive.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

(C) Process C $\rightarrow$ D(III) Zero work
(D) Net cycle A $\rightarrow$ B $\rightarrow$ C $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ A

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
In a P-V diagram, the work done by a gas is the area under the process curve on the volume axis.

For the process A $\rightarrow$ B, the line is parallel to the volume axis (isobaric) and the volume increases. Since it is an expansion, the work done is positive.

For the process B $\rightarrow$ C, the line is parallel to the pressure axis (isochoric). The volume is constant ($\Delta V = 0$), so the work done is zero.

For the process C $\rightarrow$ D, the process is isobaric and the volume decreases to return to the initial volume coordinate. Since it is a compression, the work done is negative.

The net work done in a cyclic process is the area enclosed by the cycle on the P-V diagram. Since the expansion A $\rightarrow$ B occurs at a higher pressure than the compression C $\rightarrow$ D, the cycle is clockwise and the net work done by the gas is positive.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas is compressed in a cylinder such that work is done on the gas at a rate of $60\text{ W}$. Simultaneously, the internal energy of the gas decreases at a rate of $25\text{ W}$. What is the rate of heat transfer, and is heat absorbed or released by the gas?
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics in rate form:

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{dU}{dt} + \dfrac{dW}{dt}$

Since work is done on the gas, the rate of work done is negative: $\dfrac{dW}{dt} = -60\text{ W}$.

Since the internal energy decreases, its rate of change is also negative: $\dfrac{dU}{dt} = -25\text{ W}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = -25 + (-60) = -85\text{ W}$

The negative sign indicates that heat is being released by the system to the surroundings. Therefore, heat is released at a rate of $85\text{ W}$.

Answer: $85\text{ W}$, released

questions.q: An ideal gas expands in such a way that its pressure is directly proportional to the cube of its density. During this expansion process, the temperature of the gas:
questions.solution:
Let the pressure of the gas be $P$, volume be $V$, and density be $\rho$.

Given that $P \propto \rho^3$.

Since the mass of the gas is constant, density is inversely proportional to volume ($\rho \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$).

Therefore, $P \propto \dfrac{1}{V^3}$, which can be written as $PV^3 = \text{constant}$.

From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, we can substitute $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V}$.

Substituting this into the process equation:
$\left(\dfrac{nRT}{V}\right) V^3 = \text{constant}$

$T V^2 = \text{constant}$

This implies that $T \propto \dfrac{1}{V^2}$.

As the gas expands, its volume $V$ increases. Since temperature is inversely proportional to the square of the volume, the temperature of the gas decreases.

Answer: decreases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal monatomic gas undergoes a cyclic process $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow A$ as described on a Pressure-Volume ($P-V$) diagram. The cycle forms a rectangle with vertices at $A(V_0, P_0)$, $B(V_0, 2P_0)$, $C(2V_0, 2P_0)$, and $D(2V_0, P_0)$. The heat supplied to the gas during the isobaric expansion segment is:
questions.solution:
The isobaric expansion segment is the process $B \rightarrow C$, where the pressure is constant at $2P_0$ and the volume increases from $V_0$ to $2V_0$.

The work done during this process is:
$W = P\Delta V = 2P_0(2V_0 - V_0) = 2P_0V_0$

The change in internal energy for a monatomic ideal gas is:
$\Delta U = \dfrac{3}{2}nR\Delta T = \dfrac{3}{2}P\Delta V$
$\Delta U = \dfrac{3}{2}(2P_0)(V_0) = 3P_0V_0$

According to the First Law of Thermodynamics, the heat supplied is:
$Q = W + \Delta U$
$Q = 2P_0V_0 + 3P_0V_0 = 5P_0V_0$

Alternatively, using molar heat capacity at constant pressure for a monatomic gas ($C_p = \dfrac{5}{2}R$):
$Q = nC_p\Delta T = \dfrac{5}{2}P\Delta V = \dfrac{5}{2}(2P_0)(V_0) = 5P_0V_0$

Answer: $5P_0V_0$

questions.solution:
In case of a cyclic process, work done is equal to the area under the cycle and is taken to be positive if the cycle is clockwise.
$\therefore \quad$ Work done by the gas

Helium gas is a monoatomic gas.

Along the path A B$, heat supplied to the gas at constant volume,
$\therefore \Delta Q_{A B}=n C_V \Delta T=n \frac{3}{2} R \Delta T=\frac{3}{2} V_0 \Delta P=\frac{3}{2} P_0 V_0$
Along the path $B C$, heat supplied to the gas at constant pressure,
$\therefore \Delta Q_{B C}=n C_P \Delta T=n \frac{5}{2} R \Delta T=\frac{5}{2}\left(2 P_0\right) \Delta V=5 P_0 V_0$
Along the path $C D$ and $D A$, heat is rejected by the gas
$\begin{gathered}\text{ Efficiency, } \eta=\frac{\text{ Work done by the gas }}{\text{ Heat supplied to the gas }} \times 100 \\ =\frac{P_0 V_0}{\frac{3}{2} P_0 V_0+5 P_0 V_0} \times 100=\frac{200}{13}=15.4 \%\end{gathered}$

According to first law of thermodynamics $\Delta Q=\Delta U+P \Delta V$

questions.q: The temperature of source and sink of a heat engine are $127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, respectively. An inventor claims its efficiency to be $26 \%$, then
options: it is possible with high probability
it is possible with low probability
questions.solution:
Efficiency of heat engine is
$\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1} \text{$ or $} \eta=\frac{T_1-T_2}{T_1}$
Here, $T_1=273+127=400 \mathrm{ K} \begin{aligned}
& T_2=273+27=300 \mathrm{ K} \\
& \therefore \eta=\frac{400-300}{400}=\frac{100}{400}=0.25=25 \%
\end{aligned}$
Hence, $26 \%$ efficiency is impossible for a given heat engine.

options: isothermal curve slope $=$ adiabatic curve slope

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A diatomic gas $(\gamma=1.4)$ does 200 J of work when it is expanded isobarically. Find the heat given to the gas in the process.
questions.solution:
For a diatomic gas
$C_V=\frac{5}{2} R$ and $C_p=\frac{7}{2} R$
The work done in an isobaric process is
$\begin{aligned} W & =p\left(V_2-V_1\right)=n R\left(T_2-T_1\right) \\ \Rightarrow T_2-T_1 & =\frac{W}{n R}\end{aligned}$
The heat given in an isobaric process is
$\begin{aligned} Q & =n C_p\left(T_2-T_1\right) \\ n C_p \frac{W}{n R} & =\frac{7}{2} W \\ & =\frac{7}{2} \times 200 \mathrm{~J} \\ & =700 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: 1 kg of water is converted into steam at the same temperature and at 1 atm ( 100 kPa ). The density of water and steam are $1000 \mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$ and $0.6 \mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$ respectively. The latent heat of vaporisation of water is $2.25 \times 10^6 \mathrm{Jkg}^{-1}$. What will be increase in energy?
questions.solution:
The volume of 1 kg water =$\frac{1}{100} \mathrm{~m}^3$ and $volume of 1 kg steam =\frac{1}{0.6} \mathrm{~m}^3$
The increase in volume
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{0.6} \mathrm{~m}^3-\frac{1}{1000} \mathrm{~m}^3 \\ & =(1.7-0.001) \mathrm{m}^3 \\ & \cong 1.7 \mathrm{~m}^3\end{aligned}$
The work done by steam is
$\begin{aligned} W & =(100 \mathrm{kPa})\left(1.7 \mathrm{~m}^3\right) \\ & =1.7 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$
The change in intemal energy
$\begin{aligned} \Delta U & =\Delta Q-\Delta W \\ & =2.25 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~J}-1.7 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J} \\ & =208 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: For an adiabatic expansion of a mono atomic perfect gas, the volume increases by $24 \%$. What is the percentage decrease in pressure?
questions.solution:
As we know that
$\begin{aligned} p V^\gamma & =K \\ \therefore \Delta p V^\gamma+p \gamma V^{\gamma-1} \Delta V & =0\end{aligned}$
$\Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{\Delta p}{p}\right)=-\gamma\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)$
For monoatomic gas, $\gamma=\frac{5}{3}$
$\therefore \quad \frac{\Delta p}{p}=\frac{5}{3} \times 24 \%=40 \%$

questions.solution:

questions.q: In Carnot engine efficiency is $40 \%$ at hot reservoir temperature $T$. For efficiency $50 \%$, what will be temperature of hot reservoir?
questions.solution:
The efficiency of a heat engine is defined as the ratio of work done to the heat supplied, ie,
$\eta=\frac{\text{ Work done }}{\text{ Heat input }}=\frac{W}{Q}$
or $\quad \eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$
where $T_2$ is temperature of sink, and $T_1$ is temperature of hot reservoir
$\therefore \quad \frac{40}{100}=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_2}{T_1}=0.6 \Rightarrow \quad T_1=0.6 T_1$

questions.q: Which of the following processes is reversible?
options: Electrical heating of a nichrome wire
questions.solution:
(a)It is the process by which heat is transmitted from one place to another without heating the intervening medium.
Hence, it is not a reversible process.
(b) Nichrome wire is made of alloys and has high resistance. When current is passed through it, heat is produced. So, here electrical energy is converted into heat energy. Hence, it is not a reversible process.
(c) It is the process by which heat is transmitted from one point to another through a substance in the direction of fall of temperature without the actual movement of the particles of the substances themselves. Hence, it cannot be reversible.
(d) Isothermal compression is reversible, for example-Carnot cycle, Heat engine.
Thus, choice (d) is correct.

$\begin{aligned}& =Q_1-Q_2 \\& =6.0 \times 10^4-4.8 \times 10^4 \\
& =1.2 \times 10^4 \mathrm{cal}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A perfect gas is found to obey the relation $P V^{3 / 2}=$ constant during an adiabatic process. If such a gas initially at a temperature $T$, is compressed to half of its initial volume, then its final temperature will be :
questions.solution:
Gas obeys the equation
$P V^{3 / 2}=$ constant
Comparing with $P V^\gamma=$ constant
$\gamma=\frac{3}{2}$
For adiabatic process
$\begin{aligned} T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1} & =T_2 V_2^{\gamma-1} \\ T(V)^{3 / 2-1} & =T_2\left(\frac{V}{2}\right)^{3 / 2-1} \\ T_2 & =T(2)^{3 / 2-1} \\ & =(2)^{1 / 2} T\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monoatomic gas supplied the heat $Q$ very slowly keeping the pressure constant. The work done by the gas will be
questions.solution:
For monoatomic gas at constant pressure
$\frac{\Delta U}{Q}=\frac{1}{3}$ or $\quad \Delta U=\frac{Q}{3}$
Now applying first law of thermodynamics
$\begin{aligned} W & =\Delta Q-\Delta U \\ & =Q-\frac{Q}{3}=\frac{2 Q}{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the heat of 110 J is added to a gaseous system, whose internal energy is 40 J , then the amount of external work done is
questions.solution:
Heat added to the system $\Delta Q=110 \mathrm{~J}$
Internal energy $\Delta u=40 \mathrm{~J}$
External work done is given by
$\Delta W=\Delta Q-\Delta u=110-40=70 \mathrm{~J}$
